'''NGC 300''' (also known as '''Caldwell 70''' or the '''Sculptor Pinwheel Galaxy'''<ref name="interstellarum">{{cite book|last1=Stoyan|first1=Ronald|last2=Schurig|first2=Stephan|title=interstellarum Deep Sky Atlas|publisher=Cambridge University Press; Oculum-Verlag GmbH|publication-place=Erlangen|date=2014|isbn=978-1-107-50338-0|oclc=920437579|url=http://www.deep-sky-atlas.com/}}</ref>) is a [[spiral galaxy]] in the [[constellation]] [[Sculptor (constellation)|Sculptor]]. It was discovered on 5 August 1826 by [[Scotland|Scottish]] astronomer [[James Dunlop]].<ref name="selig">{{cite web | url = https://cseligman.com/text/atlas/ngc3.htm#300 | title = New General Catalogue Objects: NGC{{nbsp}}300| last = Seligman | first = Courtney | website = Celestial Atlas | access-date = 30 August 2024}}</ref> It is one of the closest galaxies to the [[Local Group]], and it most likely lies between the latter and the [[Sculptor Group]].  It is the brightest of the five main spirals in the direction of the Sculptor Group.<ref name="Rizzietal2006" /> It is inclined at an angle of 42° when viewed from [[Earth]] and shares many characteristics of the [[Triangulum Galaxy]].<ref name="Vlajićetal2009">
{{cite journal
 |author1=Vlajić, M. |author2=Bland-hawthorn, J. |author3=Freeman, K.C.
 |date=2009
 |title=The Abundance Gradient in the Extremely Faint Outer Disk of NGC 300
 |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal]]
 |volume=697 |issue=1 |pages=361–372
 |bibcode=2009ApJ...697..361V
 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/697/1/361
|arxiv = 0903.1855 |s2cid=15805386 }}</ref> It is about 94,000 light-years in diameter, somewhat smaller than the [[Milky Way]], and has an estimated mass of (2.9 ± 0.2) × 10<sup>10</sup> {{solar mass}}.<ref name="West">{{Cite journal|last1=Westmeier|first1=T.|last2=Braun|first2=R.|last3=Koribalski|first3=B. S.|date=2011-02-01|title=Gas and dark matter in the Sculptor group: NGC 300|journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|volume=410|issue=4|pages=2217–2236|doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2010.17596.x|doi-access=free |arxiv=1009.0317|bibcode=2011MNRAS.410.2217W|s2cid=119264221}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://annesastronomynews.com/photo-gallery-ii/galaxies-clusters/ngc-300/|title = NGC 300, a spiral galaxy in Sculptor|date = 8 July 2014}}</ref>

==Nearby galaxies and group information==
NGC 300 and the [[Magellanic spiral galaxy|Magellanic type]] [[barred spiral galaxy]] [[NGC 55|NGC 55]] have traditionally been identified as members of the [[Sculptor Group]], a nearby [[group of galaxies]] in the constellation of the same name.  However, recent distance measurements indicate that these two galaxies actually lie in the foreground.<ref name="karachentsevetal2003">
{{cite journal
 |author1=Karachentsev, I.D. |display-authors=4 |author2=Grebel, E.K. |author3=Sharina, M.E.
 |author4=Dolphin, A.E. |author5=Geisler, D. |author6=Guhathakrta, P.
 |author7=Hodge, P.W. |author8=Karachentseva, V.E. |author9=Sarajedini, A.
 |author10=Seitzer, P.
 |date=2003
 |title=Distances to nearby galaxies in Sculptor
 |journal=[[Astronomy and Astrophysics]]
 |volume=404 |pages=93–111
 |bibcode=2003A&A...404...93K
 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361:20030170
 |doi-access=free|arxiv = astro-ph/0302045 |s2cid=54977869 }}</ref> It is likely that NGC 300 and NGC 55 form a gravitationally bound pair.<ref name = "vandesteeneetal2006">
{{Cite journal
 |last1=van de Steene |first1=G.C. |last2=Jacoby |first2=G.H. |last3=Praet |first3=C.
 |last4=Ciardullo |first4=R. |last5=Dejonghe |first5=H.
 |title=Distance determination to NGC 55 from the planetary nebula luminosity function
 |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics
 |date=2006
 |volume=455 |issue=3 |pages=891–896
 |bibcode=2006A&A...455..891V
 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361:20053475
|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The dwarf galaxy [[Sculptor C]] is located about 6.65 million light-years (2.04 [[megaparsec]]s) away from the Sun, and is very likely a [[satellite galaxy]] of NGC 300. Sculptor C has an absolute magnitude of about −9.1 which is typical for other recently discovered ultra-faint dwarf galaxies.<ref name=Sand2024>{{cite journal|bibcode=2024ApJ...977L...5S|arxiv=2409.16345|doi=10.3847/2041-8213/ad927c|doi-access=free |title=Three Quenched, Faint Dwarf Galaxies in the Direction of NGC 300: New Probes of Reionization and Internal Feedback |date=2024 |last1=Sand |first1=David J. |last2=Mutlu-Pakdil |first2=Burçin |last3=Jones |first3=Michael G. |last4=Karunakaran |first4=Ananthan |last5=Andrews |first5=Jennifer E. |last6=Bennet |first6=Paul |last7=Crnojević |first7=Denija |last8=Donatiello |first8=Giuseppe |last9=Drlica-Wagner |first9=Alex |last10=Fielder |first10=Catherine |last11=Martínez-Delgado |first11=David |last12=Martínez-Vázquez |first12=Clara E. |last13=Spekkens |first13=Kristine |last14=Doliva-Dolinsky |first14=Amandine |last15=Hunter |first15=Laura C. |last16=Carlin |first16=Jeffrey L. |last17=Cerny |first17=William |last18=Hai |first18=Tehreem N. |last19=McQuinn |first19=Kristen B.W. |last20=Pace |first20=Andrew B. |last21=Smercina |first21=Adam |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Letters |volume=977 |issue=1 |pages=L5 }}</ref>

==Distance estimates==
In 1986, [[Allan Sandage]] estimated the distance to NGC 300 to be 5.41 [[lightyear|Mly]] (1.66 [[Megaparsec|Mpc]]).<ref name="Sandage1986">
{{cite journal
 |last=Sandage |first=A.
 |date=1986
 |title=The redshift-distance relation. IX – Perturbation of the very nearby velocity field by the mass of the Local Group
 |journal=[[Astrophysical Journal]]
 |volume=307 |pages=1–19
 |doi=10.1086/164387
 |bibcode=1986ApJ...307....1S
|doi-access=free
 }}</ref> By 1992, this had been updated to 6.9 Mly (2.1 Mpc) by Freedman et al.<ref name="Rizzietal2006">
{{cite journal
 |author1=Rizzi, L. |display-authors=4 |author2=Bresolin, F. |author3=Kudritzki, R.-P.
 |author4=Gieren, W. |author5=Pietrzyński, G.
 |date=2006
 |title=The Araucaria Project: The Distance to NGC 300 from the Red Giant Branch Tip Using HST ACS Imaging
 |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal]]
 |volume=638 |issue=2 |pages=766–771
 |doi=10.1086/498705
 |bibcode=2006ApJ...638..766R
|arxiv = astro-ph/0510298 |s2cid=15632452 }}</ref> In 2006, this was revised by Karachentsev et al. to be {{val|7.0|0.3|u=Mly}} ({{val|2.15|0.10|u=Mpc}}).<ref name="Karachentsevetal2006">
{{cite journal
 |author1=Karachentsev, I.D. |author2=Kashibadze, O.G.
 |date=2006
 |title=Masses of the local group and of the M81 group estimated from distortions in the local velocity field
 |journal=[[Astrophysics (journal)|Astrophysics]]
 |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=3–18
 |doi=10.1007/s10511-006-0002-6
 |bibcode=2006Ap.....49....3K
|s2cid=120973010
 }}</ref> At about the same time, the [[tip of the red giant branch]] (TRGB) method was used to produce an estimate of {{val|5.9|0.4|u=Mly}} ({{val|1.82|0.13|u=Mpc}}) using edge detection and {{val|6.1|0.4|u=Mly}} ({{val|1.87|0.12|u=Mpc}}) using maximum likelihood.<ref name="Rizzietal2006" />  These results were consistent with estimates using near-infrared photometry of [[Cepheid variable]]s by Gieren et al. 2005 that provided an estimate of {{val|6.1|0.2|u=Mly}} ({{val|1.88|0.07|u=Mpc}}).<ref name="Rizzietal2006" /> Combining the recent TRGB and Cepheid estimates the distance to NGC 300 is estimated at {{val|6.07|0.23|u=Mly}} ({{val|1.86|0.07|u=Mpc}}).{{Ref_label|A|a|none}}

== Transient Events ==
AT 2019qyl was discovered by the ''Distance Less Than 40 Mpc Survey'' (DLT40) on 26 September 2019, at magnitude 17.1.  It was initially classified as a Type IIn/LBV,<ref>{{cite web | website=Transient Name Server | title=Classification certificate for object 2019qyl | url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2019qyl/classification-cert |publisher = [[International Astronomical Union|IAU]] | access-date=17 August 2024}}</ref> but later analysis classified the star as a classical [[nova]].<ref>{{cite web | website=Transient Name Server | title=AT 2019qyl | url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2019qyl |publisher = [[International Astronomical Union|IAU]] | access-date=16 August 2024}}</ref>

SN 2010da (type LBV, mag. 16) was discovered by Monard on 23 May 2010.<ref>{{cite journal |bibcode=2010CBET.2289....1M |title=Supernova 2010da in NGC 300 |last1=Monard |first1=L. A. G. |journal=Central Bureau Electronic Telegrams |date=2010 |issue=2289 |page=1 | url=http://www.cbat.eps.harvard.edu/iau/cbet/002200/CBET002289.txt}}</ref><ref name=atel2640>{{cite journal|bibcode=2010ATel.2640....1B |title=Optical Photometry of the New Optical Transient SN 2010da in NGC 300 |last1=Bond |first1=Howard E. |journal=The Astronomer's Telegram |date=2010-05-26 |volume=2640 |page=1 | url=http://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=2640}}</ref> The optical transient was detected 15".9 west and 16".8 north the center of the galaxy at coordinates 00 55 04.86 −37 41 43.7.<ref>{{cite web | website=Transient Name Server | title=SN 2010da | url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2010da | publisher = [[International Astronomical Union|IAU]] | access-date=7 June 2025}}</ref> Two sets of independent follow-up spectroscopy data suggested that this was again another optical transient rather than a supernova, possibly an outbursting [[luminous blue variable]] star according to one spectrum,<ref name=atel2636>{{cite journal |bibcode=2010ATel.2636....1E |title=SN 2010da is a SN "impostor" |last1=Elias-Rosa |first1=N. |last2=Mauerhan |first2=J. C. |last3=Van Dyk |first3=S. D. |journal=The Astronomer's Telegram |date=2010-05-25 |volume=2636 |page=1 | url=http://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=2636}}</ref><ref name=atel2637>{{cite journal |bibcode=2010ATel.2637....1C |title=Spectroscopy of SN 2010da in NGC 300 |last1=Chornock |first1=Ryan |last2=Berger |first2=Edo |journal=The Astronomer's Telegram |date=2010-05-25 |volume=2637 |page=1 |url=http://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=2637}}</ref> as earlier predicted from the nature of the candidate mid-infrared progenitor.<ref name=atel2632>{{cite journal|bibcode=2010ATel.2632....1K |title=Mid-IR progenitor of SN 2010da in NGC 300 |last1=Khan |first1=R. |last2=Stanek |first2=K. Z. |last3=Kochanek |first3=C. S. |last4=Thompson |first4=T. A. |last5=Prieto |first5=J. L. |journal=The Astronomer's Telegram |date=2010-05-24 |volume=2632 |page=1 |url=http://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=2632}}</ref>  The transient faded by 0.5–0.7 mag in 9 days, much faster than the 2008 transient in NGC 300.<ref name=atel2660>{{cite journal |bibcode=2010ATel.2660....1P |title=Optical and Near-IR Follow-up of SN 2010da: Evidence for Warm Dust |last1=Prieto |first1=J. L. |last2=Bond |first2=H. E. |last3=Kochanek |first3=C. S. |last4=Khan |first4=R. |last5=Stanek |first5=K. Z. |last6=Thompson |first6=T. A. |journal=The Astronomer's Telegram |date=2010-06-04|volume=2660 |page=1 |url=http://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=2660}}</ref>

SN 2020acli ([[Type II supernova|Type IIn-pec]], mag. 18.4205) was discovered by the ''Distance Less Than 40 Mpc Survey'' (DLT40) on 12 December 2020.<ref>{{cite web | website=Transient Name Server | title=SN 2020acli | url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2020acli | publisher = [[International Astronomical Union|IAU]] | access-date=15 January 2025}}</ref>

AT 2024oth (type unknown, mag. 19.85) was discovered by [[BlackGEM]] on 27 June 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2024oth {{!}} Transient Name Server |url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2024oth |access-date=2025-01-02 |website=www.wis-tns.org}}</ref>

AT 2024txt (type unknown, mag. 19.77) was discovered by [[Pan-STARRS]] on 29 July 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2024txt {{!}} Transient Name Server |url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2024txt |access-date=2025-01-02 |website=www.wis-tns.org}}</ref>

===NGC 300-OT===
On a [[Charge-coupled device|CCD]] image obtained on 14 May 2008, amateur astronomer L.A.G. Berto Monard discovered a bright [[optical transient]] (OT) in NGC 300 that is designated NGC 300-OT.<ref>{{cite journal|bibcode=2008IAUC.8946....1M |title=Luminous Transient in NGC 300 |last1=Monard |first1=L. A. G. |journal=International Astronomical Union Circular |date=2008 |issue=8946 |page=1 | url=http://www.cbat.eps.harvard.edu/iauc/08900/08946.html#Item1}}</ref><ref name="PrietoEtAl2009" /> It is located at [[Right ascension|RA]]: {{RA|00|54|34.552}} and [[Declination|DEC]]: {{DEC|-37|38|31.79}}<ref name="Gogartenetal2009">
{{cite journal
 |author1=Gogarten, S.M. |display-authors=4 |author2=Dalcanton, J.J. |author3=Murphy, J.W.
 |author4=Williams, B.F. |author5=Gilbert, K. |author6=Dolphin, A.
 |date=2009
 |title=The NGC 300 Transient: An Alternative Method for Measuring Progenitor Masses
 |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal]]
 |volume=703 |issue=1 |pages=300–310
 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/703/1/300
 |bibcode=2009ApJ...703..300G
|arxiv = 0907.0710 |s2cid=8131611 }}</ref> in a [[spiral arm]] containing active star formation.<ref name="Bondetal2009" /> Its broad-band magnitude was 14.3 in that image.  An earlier image (from 24 April 2008), taken just after NGC 300 reemerged from behind the [[Sun]], evidenced an already brightening OT at ~16.3 magnitude.<ref name="Bondetal2009">
{{cite journal
 |author1=Bond, H.E. |display-authors=4 |author2=Bedin, L.R. |author3=Bonanos, A.Z.
 |author4=Humphreys, R.M. |author5=Monard, L.A.G.B. |author6=Prieto, J.L.
 |author7=Water, F.M.
 |title=The 2008 Luminous Optical Transient in the Nearby Galaxy NGC 300
 |date=2009
 |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal Letters]]
 |volume=695 |issue=2 |pages=L154–L158
 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/695/2/L154
 |bibcode=2009ApJ...695L.154B
|arxiv = 0901.0198 |s2cid=15953172 }}</ref> No brightening was detected on a 8 February 2008 image, nor on any earlier ones.<ref name="Bondetal2009" /> The transient's peak measured magnitude was 14.69 on 15 May 2008.<ref name="Bondetal2009" />

At discovery, the transient had an absolute magnitude of {{nowrap|MV ≈ −13}}, making it faint in comparison to a typical [[core-collapse supernova]] but bright in comparison to a [[classical nova]].<ref name="PrietoEtAl2009" /><ref name="Bondetal2009" /> Additionally, the photometric and spectroscopic properties of the OT imply that it is not a [[luminous blue variable]] either.<ref name="Bondetal2009" /> Since its peak, brightness dropped smoothly through September 2008 while becoming continuously redder.<ref name="Bondetal2009" /> After September 2008, brightness continued to fall at a lower rate in the optical spectrum but with strong [[hydrogen alpha|Hα]] emissions.<ref name="Bondetal2009" /> Further, the optical spectrum is mostly made up of fairly narrow [[Hydrogen Balmer]] and Ca II emission lines coupled with strong Ca II H&K absorption.<ref name="PrietoEtAl2009" />  Research into historical [[Hubble Space Telescope|Hubble]] images provide an accurate upper bound on the progenitor star's brightness.<ref name="PrietoEtAl2009" /> This suggested a low-mass [[main sequence]] star as progenitor with the transient resulting from a stellar merger similar to red Galactic nova [[V838 Monocerotis]].<ref name="PrietoEtAl2009">
{{cite journal
 |date=2009
 |title=A Spitzer/IRS Spectrum of the 2008 Luminous Transient in NGC 300: Connection to Proto-Planetary Nebulae
 |last1=Prieto   | first1=J.L.
 |last2=Sellgren |first2=K.
 |last3=Thompson | first3=T.A.
 |last4=Kochanek | first4=C.S.
 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/705/2/1425
 |journal=The Astrophysical Journal
 |volume=705
 |issue=2
 |pages=1425–1432
 |arxiv=0907.0230
|bibcode = 2009ApJ...705.1425P |s2cid=15627891
 }}</ref> Analysis of historical images of the area of the OT suggest with 70% certainty that the progenitor formed in a burst of stars around 8–13 Myr ago and implies the progenitor's mass to be 12–25 [[solar mass|M<sub>☉</sub>]] assuming the OT is due to an evolving massive star.<ref name="Gogartenetal2009" />

[[File:NGC 300 Hubble.jpg|thumb|NGC 300 zoom-in by the [[Hubble Space Telescope]]]]
[[file:Composite Image of NGC 300.jpg|thumb|NGC 300 by [[GALEX]], in ultraviolet light]]
However, in 2008 a bright [[mid-infrared]] progenitor to the transient was discovered in historical [[Spitzer Space Telescope|Spitzer]] data. This was a star that was obscured by dust, with energy distribution analogous to a [[black-body]] of {{nowrap|''R'' ≈ 300}} [[astronomical units|AU]] and radiating at {{nowrap|''T'' ≈ 300}} [[kelvin|K]] with {{nowrap|''L''<sub>bol</sub> ≈ {{e|6|4}} [[solar luminosity|''L''<sub>☉</sub>]]}}. This demonstrated that the transient was associated with an energetic explosion of a low-mass ≈ 10 M<sub>☉</sub> star. The transient's low luminosity as compared to typical core-collapse supernova, combined with its spectral attributes and dust covered properties, make it nearly identical to [[NGC 6946|NGG 6946]]'s [[SN 2008S|SN 2008S]].<ref name="PrietoEtAl2009" />

The spectrum of NGC 300-OT observed with Spitzer shows strong, broad emission features at 8 μm and 12 μm.  Such features are also seen in Galactic [[carbon star|carbon-rich]] [[protoplanetary nebulae]].<ref name="PrietoEtAl2009" />

On 19 April 2025, NGC 300-OT was classified as an Intermediate-Luminosity Red Transient (ILRT).<ref>{{cite web | website=Transient Name Server | title=Classification certificate for object 2008jd | url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2008jd/classification-cert | publisher = [[International Astronomical Union|IAU]] | access-date=19 April 2025}}</ref>

==Astronomical objects==
===Binary black hole system===
[[File:Artist’s impression of the black hole inside NGC 300 X-1 (ESO 1004a).jpg|thumb|Artistic representation of NGC 300 X-1 system]]

An [[x-ray astronomy|x-ray]] source in NGC 300 is designated NGC 300 X-1.<ref name = "Barnardetal2008" />  Astronomers speculate that NGC 300 X-1 is a new kind of [[Wolf–Rayet star|Wolf-Rayet]] + [[stellar black hole]] [[binary system (astronomy)|binary system]] similar to the confirmed such system [[IC 10|IC 10]] X-1.<ref name = "Barnardetal2008">
{{cite journal
 |author1=Barnard, R. |author2=Clark, J.S. |author3=Kolb, U.C.
 |date=2008
 |title=NGC 300 X-1 and IC 10 X-1: a new breed of black hole binary?
 |journal=[[Astronomy and Astrophysics]]
 |volume=488 |issue=2 |pages=697–703
 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361:20077975
  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2008A&A...488..697B
|arxiv = 0807.0606 |s2cid=1234999 }}</ref> Their shared properties include an [[orbital period]] of 32.8 hours. The black hole has a mass of 17 ± 4 {{Solar mass|link=true}} and the WR star has a mass of {{Val|26|7|5}} {{Solar mass}}. Both objects orbit each other at a distance of about 18.2 {{Solar radius|link=true}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Binder |first1=Breanna A. |last2=Sy |first2=Janelle M. |last3=Eracleous |first3=Michael |last4=Christodoulou |first4=Dimitris M. |last5=Bhattacharya |first5=Sayantan |last6=Cappallo |first6=Rigel |last7=Laycock |first7=Silas |last8=Plucinsky |first8=Paul P. |last9=Williams |first9=Benjamin F. |date=2021-03-01 |title=The Wolf–Rayet + Black Hole Binary NGC 300 X-1: What is the Mass of the Black Hole? |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=910 |issue=1 |pages=74 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/abe6a9 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2102.07065 |bibcode=2021ApJ...910...74B |issn=0004-637X}}</ref>

=== WO star ===
There is an oxygen-sequence Wolf–Rayet star (WO4 type), known as STWR 13, located in one of the bright H II regions in NGC 300.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Breysacher |first1=J. |last2=Azzopardi |first2=M. |last3=Testor |first3=G. |last4=Muratorio |first4=G. |date=1997-10-01 |title=Wolf–Rayet stars detected in five associations of NGC 300. |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1997A&A...326..976B |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics |volume=326 |pages=976–981 |bibcode=1997A&A...326..976B |issn=0004-6361}}</ref>

'''Dwingeloo 1''' is a [[barred spiral galaxy]] about 10 million [[light-year]]s away from the Earth,<ref name=Karachentsev2005/> in the [[constellation]] [[Cassiopeia (constellation)|Cassiopeia]].  It lies in the [[Zone of Avoidance]] and is heavily obscured by the [[Milky Way]]. The size and mass of Dwingeloo 1 are comparable to those of [[Triangulum Galaxy]].

Dwingeloo 1 has two smaller [[satellite galaxy|satellite galaxies]] – [[Dwingeloo 2]] and [[MB 3]] – and is a member of the [[IC 342/Maffei Group]] of galaxies.

==Discovery==
The Dwingeloo 1 galaxy was discovered in 1994 by the Dwingeloo Obscured Galaxy Survey (DOGS) using the [[Dwingeloo Radio Observatory]], which searched for neutral hydrogen (HI) radio emissions at the wavelength of 21 cm from objects in the [[Zone of Avoidance]]. In this zone gas and dust in the disk of the [[Milky Way]] galaxy block the light from the galaxies lying behind it.<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994/>

The galaxy was, however, first noted as an unremarkable feature on [[Palomar Sky Survey]] plates earlier in the same year, but was not recognized as such.<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kraan-Korteweg | first1 = R. C. | last2 = Loan | first2 = A. J. | last3 = Burton | first3 = W. B. | last4 = Lahav | first4 = O. | last5 = Ferguson | first5 = H. C. | last6 = Henning | first6 = P. A. | last7 = Lynden-Bell | first7 = D. | doi = 10.1038/372077a0 | title = Discovery of a nearby spiral galaxy behind the Milky Way | journal = Nature | volume = 372 | issue = 6501 | pages = 77 | year = 1994 |bibcode = 1994Natur.372...77K | s2cid = 4242688 }}</ref> It was also independently discovered a few weeks later by another team of astronomers working with [[Effelsberg 100-m Radio Telescope]].<ref name=Huchtmeier1995/>

Dwingeloo 1 was eventually named after the [[Dwingeloo Radio Observatory|25m radio telescope]] in the [[Netherlands]] that was used in the DOGS survey and first detected it.<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994/>

==Distance and group membership==
Dwingeloo 1 is a highly obscured galaxy, which makes distance determination a difficult problem. The initial estimate, made soon after the discovery and based on the [[Tully–Fisher relation]], was about 3 Mpc.<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994/> Later, this value was slightly increased to 3.5–4 Mpc.<ref name=Loan1996/>

In 1999 another estimate was published, claiming a distance of more than 5 Mpc. It was based on the infrared Tully–Fisher relation.<ref name=Ivanov1999>{{Cite journal | last1 = Ivanov | first1 = V. D. | last2 = Alonso-Herrero | first2 = A.|author2-link=Almudena Alonso-Herrero | last3 = Rieke | first3 = M. J. | last4 = McCarthy | first4 = D. | title = An Infrared Determination of the Reddening and Distance to Dwingeloo 1 | doi = 10.1086/300986 | journal = The Astronomical Journal | volume = 118 | issue = 2 | pages = 826 | year = 1999 |arxiv = astro-ph/9905152 |bibcode = 1999AJ....118..826I | s2cid = 15619332 }}</ref> As of 2011, the distance to Dwingeloo 1 is thought to be approximately 3 Mpc, based on its likely membership in the IC 342/Maffei group.<ref name=Karachentsev2005>{{Cite journal | last1 = Karachentsev | first1 = I. D. | doi = 10.1086/426368 | title = The Local Group and Other Neighboring Galaxy Groups | journal = The Astronomical Journal | volume = 129 | pages = 178–188 | year = 2005 | issue = 1 |arxiv = astro-ph/0410065 |bibcode = 2005AJ....129..178K | s2cid = 119385141 }}</ref>

Dwingeloo 1 has two smaller [[satellite galaxy|satellite galaxies]]. The first one, [[Dwingeloo 2]], is an [[irregular galaxy]],<ref name=Burton1996/> and the second, [[MB 3]], is likely a [[dwarf spheroidal galaxy]].

==Properties==
After the discovery Dwingeloo 1 was classified as a [[barred spiral galaxy]].<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994/> It has a central bar and two distinct [[spiral arm]]s that begin at the ends of the bar at nearly right angles and wind counterclockwise. The length of the arms is up to 180°.<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994/> The disk of the galaxy is inclined with respect to the observer, with the inclination angle being 50°. The galaxy recedes from the Milky Way at a speed of about 256 km/s.<ref name=Loan1996/>

The visible radius of Dwingeloo 1 is approximately 4.2', which at the distance of 3 Mpc corresponds to about 4 kpc. The neutral hydrogen is detected as far as 6 kpc (7.5') from the center. The total mass of the galaxy is about 1/4 that of the Milky Way out to the measured distance of 6 kpc or about 31 billion Solar masses.<ref name=Burton1996/>

The distribution of the neutral hydrogen in Dwingeloo 1 is typical for barred spiral galaxies—it is rather flat with a minimum in the center or along the bar.<ref name=Burton1996/> The total mass of the neutral hydrogen is estimated at 370–450 million [[Solar mass]]es.<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994/><ref name=Huchtmeier1995/> Dwingeloo 1 is a molecular gas-poor galaxy. The total mass of the [[molecular hydrogen]] does not exceed 10% of that of neutral hydrogen.<ref name=Kuno1996/> Optical observations detected around 15 [[H II region]]s situated mainly along the spiral arms.<ref name=Loan1996/>

In its overall size and mass, the galaxy is comparable to [[Triangulum Galaxy]].<ref name=Kraan-Korteweg1994/>

'''Sextans B''' (also known as '''UGC 5373''' and '''DDO 70''') is an [[irregular galaxy|irregular]] [[galaxy]] that may be part of the [[Local Group]], or lie just beyond it. The earliest known reference to this galaxy is from a 1954 paper by [[Edison Pettit]] in [[The Astrophysical Journal]], where it was listed as "Wilson Dwarf".<ref>{{cite journal|bibcode=1954ApJ...120..413P |title=Magnitudes and Color Indices of Extragalactic Nebulae Determined Photoelectrically |last1=Pettit |first1=Edison |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=1954 |volume=120 |page=413 |doi=10.1086/145932 }}</ref>

Sextans B is 4.44 million [[light-year]]s away from [[Earth]] and thus is one of the most distant members of the Local Group, if it is indeed a member. It forms a pair with its neighbouring galaxy [[Sextans A]].<ref name="SandageCarlson1985"/> It is a type Ir IV–V galaxy according to the [[galaxy morphological classification]] scheme.<ref name="vandenBergh2000"/> Sextans B may also be gravitationally associated with the galaxies [[NGC 3109]] and the [[Antlia Dwarf]].<ref name="vandenbergh1999"/>

Sextans B has a uniform stellar population,<ref name="TosiEtAl1991"/> but the interstellar medium in it may be inhomogeneous.<ref name="KniazevEtAl2005"/> Its mass is estimated to be about 2{{e|8}} times the mass of the [[Sun]], of which 5.5{{e|7}} is in the form of atomic [[hydrogen]].<ref name="TosiEtAl1991"/> Star formation in the galaxy seems to have proceeded in distinct periods of low intensity, separated by shorter periods of no activity.<ref name="TosiEtAl1991"/> The existence of [[Cepheid variable]]s in the galaxy implies that Sextans B contains at least some young stars.<ref name="vandenBergh2000"/> The [[metallicity]] of Sextans B is very low, with a value of approximately Z = 0.001.<ref name="TosiEtAl1991"/> Sextans B is receding from the [[Milky Way]] with a speed of approximately {{convert|300|km/s|mi/s}},<ref name="KniazevEtAl2005"/> and probably lies just outside the edge of the [[Local Group]], so as its neighbour [[Sextans A]].<ref name="AlloinGieren"/>

Five [[planetary nebula]]e have been identified in Sextans B, which is one of the smallest galaxies where planetary nebulae have been observed. These appear point-like and can be identified by their spectral emission lines.<ref name="MagriniEtAl2002"/> It also contains a massive [[globular cluster]].<ref name="SharinaEtAl2007"/>

Although no [[supernova]]e have been observed in Sextans B, the galaxy is close enough for classical [[nova]]e to be detected. The first confirmed nova in this galaxy was discovered by [[Asteroid_Terrestrial-impact_Last_Alert_System|ATLAS]] at magnitude 18.553 on 10 November 2024, and designated AT 2024aawe.<ref>{{cite web | website=Transient Name Server | title=AT{{nbsp}}2024aawe | url=https://www.wis-tns.org/object/2024aawe | publisher = [[International_Astronomical_Union|IAU]] | access-date=12 November 2024}}</ref>

== Characteristics ==
[[File:NGC4214 JeffJohnson.jpg|thumb|left|Amateur image of NGC 4214]]

NGC 4214 is both larger and brighter than the [[Small Magellanic Cloud]]<ref name="Karachentsev2004">{{cite journal
    | author=Karachentsev, Igor D. | author2=Karachentseva, Valentina E. | author3=Huchtmeier, Walter K. | author4=Makarov, Dmitry I.
    | title=A Catalog of Neighboring Galaxies
    | journal=The Astronomical Journal
    | date=2003
    | volume=127
    | issue=4
    | pages=2031–2068
    | bibcode=2004AJ....127.2031K
    | doi=10.1086/382905| doi-access=free
    }}</ref> as well as a [[starburst galaxy]], with the largest star-forming regions (''NGC 4214-I'' and ''NGC 4214-II'') in the galaxy's center. Of the two, ''NGC 4214-I'' contains a [[super star cluster]] rich in [[Wolf–Rayet star]]s and ''NGC 4214-II'' is younger (age less than 3 million years), including a number of [[star cluster]]s and [[stellar association]]s.<ref name="Ubeda2004">{{cite journal
    | author=Ubeda, L. | author2=Maíz-Apellániz, J. | author3=MacKenty, J. W.
    | title=Massive Young Star Clusters in NGC 4214
    | journal=The Formation and Evolution of Massive Young Star Clusters, ASP Conference Series |editor=H.J.G.L.M. Lamers |editor2=L.J. Smith |editor3=A. Nota|editor3-link=Antonella Nota | date=2004
    | volume=322
    | pages=221
    | bibcode=2004ASPC..322..221U
     }}</ref>

NGC 4214 also has two older super star clusters, both with an age of 200 million years and respective masses of {{val|2.6|e=5}} and {{val|1.5|e=6}} [[solar mass]]es.<ref name="Larsen2004">{{cite journal
    | author=Larsen, Søren S. | author2=Brodie, Jean P. | author3=Hunter, Deidre A. |author-link3=Deidre Hunter
    | title=Dynamical Mass Estimates for Five Young Massive Stellar Clusters
    | journal=The Astronomical Journal
    | date=2004
    | volume=128
    | issue=5
    | pages=2295–2305
    | bibcode=2004AJ....128.2295L
    | doi=10.1086/424538|arxiv = astro-ph/0407373 | s2cid=36220968 }}</ref>

Two satellites are known to exist around the vicinity of NGC 4214. One is DDO 113, which has an absolute V-band magnitude of −12.2. It stopped star formation around 1 billion years ago. Another, more recently discovered object is MADCASH-2, officially named MADCASH J121007+352635-dw. The name refers to the MADCASH (Magellanic Analog Dwarf Companions and Stellar Halos) project. It is similar to typical ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, with an absolute V-band magnitude of −9.15, except in that it shows evidence of multiple episodes of star formation in its recent past: one around 400 million years ago, and another 1.5 billion years ago.<ref name=Carlin2021>{{cite journal|doi=10.3847/1538-4357/abe040|arxiv=2012.09174|bibcode=2021ApJ...909..211C|title=Hubble Space Telescope Observations of Two Faint Dwarf Satellites of Nearby LMC Analogs from MADCASH|year=2021|last1=Carlin|first1=Jeffrey L.|last2=Mutlu-Pakdil|first2=Burçin|last3=Crnojević|first3=Denija|last4=Garling|first4=Christopher T.|last5=Karunakaran|first5=Ananthan|last6=Peter|first6=Annika H. '''Leo P''' is a small, star-forming [[irregular galaxy]] located in the constellation [[Leo (constellation)|Leo]], discovered through the blind HI Arecibo Legacy Fast ALFA ([[ALFALFA]]) survey, as an ultra-compact [[high-velocity cloud]] (UCHVC) of hydrogen gas. Its confirmation as a [[dwarf galaxy]] in 2013 suggests that other such UCHVCs are possibly undiscovered dwarf galaxies themselves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Faerman |first=Yakov |last2=Sternberg |first2=Amiel |last3=McKee |first3=Christopher F. |date=2013-11-01 |title=Ultra-compact High Velocity Clouds as Minihalos and Dwarf Galaxies |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...777..119F |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=777 |pages=119 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/777/2/119 |issn=0004-637X|arxiv=1309.0815 }}</ref> Leo P is noteworthy for harbouring one of the most metal-poor environments in the local universe. Its metallicity is just 3% that of the Sun's, meaning that its stars contain 30 times less heavy elements than the Sun.<ref name="mcquinn" /> This makes Leo P similar to the pristine environments of primordial galaxies.

Leo P is located on the very outskirts of the [[Local Group]], nearly 5.3 million light years away, and may not be part of it, instead being part of the [[Antlia-Sextans Group]], a small grouping of galaxies adjacent to the Local Group, sometimes considered bound to it.

==Properties==
[[File:Leo P imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope.jpg|thumb|left|This [[James Webb Space Telescope]] image shows a portion of the Leo P dwarf galaxy.]]
Leo P is one of the smallest, least massive and faintest star-forming galaxies in the [[Local Group]]. Its total luminosity is less than 440,000 times that of the Sun ([[absolute magnitude]] of −9.27), and its stellar mass is only about 560,000 [[solar mass]]es, implying a small stellar population. Leo P is also very rich in gas, containing about 810,000 solar masses of neutral hydrogen.<ref name=mcquinn/> Leo P's [[Galaxy effective radius|half-light radius]] is about 570 pc.<ref name=putman/> Early attempts to detect [[molecular hydrogen]] in Leo P were unsuccessful. In 2025 [[James Webb Space Telescope]] discovered rotational emission lines of H<sub>2</sub> in the [[mid-infrared]] part of the spectra leading to an estimate of the molecular hydrogen mass of the galaxy >10<sup>4</sup> solar masses.<ref name="Telford 2025">{{cite journal |last1=Telford |first1=O. Grace |last2=Sandstrom |first2=Karin M. |last3=McQuinn |first3=Kristen B. W. |last4=Glover |first4=Simon C. O. |last5=Tarantino |first5=Elizabeth J. |last6=Bolatto |first6=Alberto D. |last7=Rickards Vaught |first7=Ryan J. |title=Molecular hydrogen in the extremely metal- and dust-poor galaxy Leo P |journal=Nature |date=11 June 2025 |doi=10.1038/s41586-025-09115-7}}</ref>

Leo P's stellar population consists of a strong concentration of massive, bright and [[OB star|blue stars]] in the centre of the galaxy, which may be B and A-type [[main sequence]] stars. Some fainter and redder stars are also observed, presumably [[red giant]]s from an older [[stellar population]].<ref name=rhode/> 10 [[RR Lyrae star]]s have been detected in the galaxy, as well as one [[H II region]], which is ionised by LP26, an [[O-type star]] of 22 solar masses, the only one in Leo P.<ref name=telford/>
 
=== Star formation ===
Leo P is one of the few [[Local Group]] galaxies which are currently forming stars. Its star formation rate is about {{val|4.3|e=-5|ul=M_solar}} every year,<ref name=mcquinn/> or 1 solar mass every 20,400 years, and it is the Local Group's most metal-poor star-forming galaxy. Its star formation history shows mostly constant star formation throughout its lifetime, something which is also observed in larger irregular galaxies. Models also suggest that there was not much star formation post-reionisation, 12–8 billion years ago, and over the last 4 billion years, star formation has been happening at a constant rate.<ref name=mcquinn/>

'''UGC 9128''' is a [[Dwarf galaxy|dwarf]] [[Irregular galaxy|irregular]] [[galaxy]] around 6.8–7.8 [[light-year|Mly]] (2.1–2.4 [[parsec|Mpc]]) away; it is thought to be in the [[Local Group]], although its membership is not certain.<ref name="telescope1">{{cite web |title=Dwarf galaxy: small but perfectly formed |url=https://esahubble.org/images/potw1117a/ |website=www.spacetelescope.org |access-date=8 August 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="starburst1"/> The galaxy has a mass of about {{val|1.3|0.2|e=7|u={{solar mass}}}}, around 100 million [[stars]], and a diameter of around 3300 [[light-year|ly]].<ref name="starburst1"/><ref name="slate1">{{cite web |last1=Plait |first1=Phil |title=And the cottonball galaxies shall inherit the Universe |url=https://slate.com/technology/2011/04/and-the-cottonball-galaxies-shall-inherit-the-universe.html |website=Slate Magazine |access-date=8 August 2021 |language=en |date=25 April 2011}}</ref> It is therefore quite faint, and so was only discovered in the 20th century.<ref name="telescope1" />

UGC 9128 is around 2.7 [[light-year|Mly]] from [[GR 8 (galaxy)|GR 8]], which is its nearest neighbour.<ref name="ddo1" />

UGC 9128 is a [[starburst galaxy]], with the peak of star formation being 20–100 million years ago.<ref name="starburst1"/><ref name="ddo1" /> It is thought to have both a [[galactic halo|halo]] and [[galactic disc|disc]].<ref name="ddo1" />
